extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, recruitment officers, and Army administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal standards, statutory rules, and case law governing enlistment, reenlistment, and classification of service (especially the requirement of "honest and faithful" service, fraudulent enlistment, and the Government's remedies). Aimed at determining validity of enlistments and entitlement to reenlistment/benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service presumed honest and faithful unless contrary established
rubrics_metrics.description: Service honest and faithful unless contrary is established; "service not honest and faithful" remark will not be entered except after action of a board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act of August 1, 1894 provides that no soldier shall be reenlisted whose service in last preceding term was not honest and faithful. Service is presumed honest and faithful until the soldier's conduct renders it otherwise. Examples/notes: last term may have been in volunteers; a felon pardoned and returned to duty may have service held honest and faithful in some cases; a board action is required to record "service not honest and faithful."

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion does not automatically negate honest and faithful service
rubrics_metrics.description: Desertion does not necessarily render service 'not honest and faithful' for purposes of reenlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether desertion negates honest and faithful service depends on the facts of each case. A deserter restored to duty without trial may still have service classified as honest and faithful; a convicted deserter not sentenced to dishonorable discharge may still have honest and faithful service in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bar to reenlistment for prior term not honest and faithful (Act of Aug. 1, 1894)
rubrics_metrics.description: No soldier shall be reenlisted whose service in last preceding term was not honest and faithful (Act of August 1, 1894, 28 Stat. 216).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application involves fact-specific determinations (e.g., pardons, remissions, convictions). Even where statute applies, Secretary/boards may exercise discretion in classification; prior good service during last term may mitigate statutory effect in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardons and remission do not necessarily restore prior service character
rubrics_metrics.description: A pardon or remission of unexecuted sentence does not render previous service honest and faithful; a pardon does not change previous character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: remission of unexecuted sentence of a felon does not render previous service honest and faithful; remission for a military convict deserter similarly does not restore honest service. Restoration to citizenship or pardon of a dishonorably discharged soldier does not render prior service honest and faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge generally makes prior service not honest and faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonorably discharged soldier's service is not honest and faithful; a discharged military convict's service is not honest and faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, after mitigation of a deserter's sentence of dishonorable discharge, the soldier may receive an honorable discharge with service characterized as honest and faithful. Classification depends on circumstances and may involve board or Secretary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War discretion to classify service as honest and faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War has discretion to classify service as honest and faithful for the purpose of reenlistment except where service is clearly not honest and faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative categories where discretion applies: honorable discharge recorded as not honest and faithful; deserter restored to duty without trial; soldier discharged without honor (after board action or otherwise); convicted deserter not sentenced to dishonorable discharge; discharged military convict. The Secretary cannot properly determine cases as honest and faithful when the offense ordinarily calls for dishonorable discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory classification for extra pay for service outside U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of January 12, 1899 and March 3, 1899 authorize extra pay to officers and enlisted men who served honestly and faithfully outside the limits of the United States and require classification of manner and character of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules/regulations aid classification. Examples: soldier absent without leave, drunk, or who died—service not honest and faithful; officer confessed embezzlement—service not honest and faithful; an officer tried by court-martial may nevertheless have service classified as honest and faithful in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlistment is a contract for military service; evidence of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlistment is a contract entered into between a civilian and the Government; any acts indicating an undertaking to render military service and acceptance by the Government may be legal evidence of a contract of enlistment and equivalent to a formal agreement where none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The receipt of pay by a party as a soldier is evidence of enlistment. Continuing performance of accepted service may constitute constructive enlistment, even when formal writings are absent. Cases: mustering out and immediate reenlistment does not force a new contract; acceptance under Presidential conditional pardons may constitute enlistment for agreed period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath not essential to validity of enlistment though customary
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking of the oath prescribed by the second article of war is not essential to the validity of an enlistment, though it is almost invariably part of a regular formal enlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases hold formal oath customary but not necessary for legal enlistment. Practical implication: absence of the oath does not automatically invalidate an enlistment if other indicia of contract/acceptance exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruit's declaration of age is not part of the oath; false age declaration not perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: A recruit's declaration as to his age is no part of the oath prescribed by the second article of war; there is no law requiring such declaration to be under oath, and a false declaration as to age is not indictable for perjury under section 5392, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences for false age statements are addressed under enlistment/fraud rules rather than as perjury; separate statutory provisions govern minors and parental consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued rendering and acceptance of service can constitute enlistment (constructive enlistment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The continued rendering of service which is accepted may constitute an enlistment even absent formalities; enlistment may be evidenced by acceptance and payment for services performed as a soldier (constructive enlistment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: officer revoked appointment returns to private service and, by compliance and acceptance of pay, is constructively enlisted. The Government's acceptance converts the relationship into soldier status until discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlistments on Sunday are valid
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law or regulation affecting the validity of an enlistment made on Sunday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cases uphold Sunday enlistments as valid. Administrative practice recognizes no invalidity based solely on day of week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may change pay/allowances during enlistment by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagements of officers and soldiers are subject to the right of the Government to change by law their pay and allowances in its discretion; a contract of enlistment is not violated by lawful reduction of pay by act of Congress while the enlistment is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law supports that statutory changes in pay do not breach the enlistment contract. Recruiters/administrators must account for lawful legislative changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: President cannot accept enlistment conditioned on service in specified region
rubrics_metrics.description: No statute authorizes the President to accept into or retain an individual in the military service on a condition that he shall be sent to this or that part of the country to serve; such agreements would be impracticable and inconsistent with public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative practice should not create binding geographic-condition enlistments; such conditions are legally ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer recruits into U.S. Volunteers enlist directly into U.S. service
rubrics_metrics.description: Under laws relating to raising a volunteer army, recruits for the United States Volunteers are enlisted directly into the service of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War authorized to prescribe rules and regulations for examining, organizing, and receiving volunteers. Historical General Orders and statutes cited govern volunteer enlistments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date in oath is controlling enlistment date; proof of date not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The date set forth in the oath is the date on which a soldier is enlisted within the meaning of the Articles of War; proof of the date of enlistment is not essential to proof of enlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative practice allows relating acceptance back to the applicant's date where delay in final acceptance was not the applicant's fault, to preserve continuous service. Numerous cases recognize the oath date as controlling for enlistment date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed acceptance may relate back to preserve continuous service
rubrics_metrics.description: Where application for reenlistment made within the legal time but final acceptance delayed without fault of the applicant, it is permissible to have the final acceptance relate back to and take effect on the date of the applicant's acceptance so the soldier may be considered as having continuous service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cases and Army Regulations permit this remedy; exceptions exist (e.g., medical operations leading to failure to reenlist within limit cannot be antedated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fraudulent enlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: A fraudulent enlistment is an enlistment procured by means of a willful misrepresentation regarding a qualification or disqualification for enlistment, or by an intentional concealment of a disqualification, which misrepresentation or concealment caused the enlistment of a man not qualified to be a soldier and who, but for such false representation or concealment, would have been rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition (published in circulars/decisions) is applied in cases determining whether enlistment is voidable and whether offenses have been committed. Examples include concealment of felony conviction or prior desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization and elements of fraudulent enlistment (Act of July 27, 1892)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the act of July 27, 1892, fraudulent enlistment was not necessarily a military offense; the act made fraudulent enlistment a military offense and made receipt of pay and allowances a part of the offense. To complete the offense, entry into the service by misrepresentation and the receipt of pay and allowances are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law interprets the statute: both procurement by fraud and receipt of pay are required for court-martial jurisdiction. Historical decisions discuss constitutionality and interaction with contract law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent enlistments are generally voidable, not void
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections prohibiting enlistment of deserters, convicted felons, insane persons, intoxicated persons, certain minors, etc., are directory only and render such enlistments voidable at the option of the Government rather than automatically void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voids/voidable distinction: until avoided, the enlistment is valid and the soldier is subject to obligations (e.g., may be tried for offenses committed while enlisted). Exceptions for insanity, idiocy, infancy, or other causes that disable a party from changing status may lead to different results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government remedies for fraudulent enlistment (options and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where fraudulent enlistment is established, the Government may (at its option) try the individual for fraudulent enlistment, summarily discharge him without honor, restore him to duty, or permit him to serve out the enlistment; the choice is the Government's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy: the War Department often retains a man with good subsequent service. If the soldier was tried and not sentenced to dishonorable discharge, the Government should not also summarily discharge him (avoiding double punishment). Cases outline options and equitable considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules and consequences for minors who enlist fraudulently or without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The enlistment of a minor over 16 without the written consent of parent/guardian is not void but voidable; enlistment of a minor under 16 may be void in some authorities but generally is treated as voidable depending on capacity. A minor who conceals his age and receives pay may be retained, discharged without honor, tried for fraudulent enlistment, honorably discharged, or restored to duty in the Secretary's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions acknowledge that until avoided, the minor is a soldier and may be tried for offenses; parents/guardians or the Government may avoid the enlistment. Administrative orders and cases cited (In re Morrissey, In re Grimley, etc.) provide guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent enlistment by deserters, discharged convicts, or prior service offenders
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter, a person dishonorably discharged, or a discharged convict who fraudulently enlists may be subject to trial for desertion and fraudulent enlistment, summarily discharged without honor, restored to duty, or held to serve the fraudulent enlistment or original enlistment at the Government's option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deserters who enlist elsewhere by concealment commit fraudulent enlistment; the Government may elect the remedy (trial, retention, or discharge). Departmental practice historically leans toward retaining those who thereafter have good service records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service under a fraudulent enlistment counts for benefits unless the enlistment is avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Time actually served under a fraudulent enlistment should be counted in computing service (e.g., toward the 30 years necessary for retirement) and counts toward continuous service unless the enlistment is voided as fraudulent by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cases hold that unless the Government has avoided the contract for fraud, the service is legal and entitles the soldier to benefits accrued during that period (retirement credit, certificates of merit, pay increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and pay to soldiers who served under fraudulent enlistment may be lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: The award of a certificate of merit to a soldier serving under a fraudulent enlistment is lawful, and if restored to duty without trial he may be entitled to additional pay authorized by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law upholds payment and honors granted for service performed under fraudulent enlistments when the Government has not avoided the enlistment; practical implication is that remedial action (voiding enlistment) is necessary to deny such benefits.
